# Changelog

## 0.2.0

The CLI moves onto go-strictcli v0.33.0: presence is declared at every flag and argument, a command that writes may no longer default a value, and `strictcode fix` takes its apply-or-preview decision as a required selector rather than a pair of booleans.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

Three v0.33.0 registration rules reach this CLI, and two of them needed a judgment the framework cannot make.

The mutating-default ban says absence must never resolve to a value the invocation did not state, because on a command that writes, a value the framework picked is a value the framework writes. Four declarations were refused. All four are paths -- a search root or a destination, never a value that lands inside an artifact -- so each moved its fallback into the handler and states it in `--help`, which is the remedy the rule names for exactly this case. `analyze` reads and never writes, so its declared defaults are untouched.

`MutexGroup` no longer exists; exactly-one selection is a choice flag. The `fix` command's apply-or-preview pair became a member-spelled selector rather than a token one, because the two options were already spelled as their own flags and a token selector would have rewritten the command line for no reason the rule asked for. It also closes a real hole: under the old boolean mutex `--no-apply` satisfied the group while electing nothing, so a negation could be read as a request for the other option. A member is elected by presence, so that input is now refused.

No command declares an update record. Each of the three would have had to invent a property flag that does not exist -- `fix`'s edits come from the graph, and the two generators rewrite a whole artifact -- and the reasoning is recorded at each registration site so a later reader does not re-open it as an oversight.

</details>

### Breaking

- **Breaking: `strictcode fix` takes its apply-or-preview decision as a required selector.** `--apply` and `--preview` are spelled exactly as before and exactly one is still mandatory, but they are now elected by presence: `--no-apply` and `--no-preview` are refused rather than quietly standing in for the other option. Absence no longer resolves to a tool-picked value on any command that writes — `fix`'s directory and `--config`, and `registry dump`/`matrix gen`'s `--out`, apply their fallbacks in the handler and state them in `--help`.

## 0.1.0

First release: architecture linter with a working seed catalog (dependency hygiene, dead code, cycles, library boundaries) across Python, Go, and TypeScript/JavaScript at import-graph depth, Python full-semantic depth, and tier-1 guaranteed-safe auto-fixes with graph re-verification.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

strictcode absorbs the source-analysis duties rlsbl is shedding (rlsbl never parses source). The graph model is an interaction relation with qualified node identity; rules are built-in Go code with mint-once IDs and a generated language-by-feature support matrix; all schema artifacts are strictspec-gated documents. The 32-item lessons register from the donor implementation is fully covered by red-green regression tests, plus five new lessons minted from real-corpus contact.

</details>

### Breaking

- **Breaking: machine output is now the strictcli envelope, entered with `--json`.** `strictcode analyze` no longer takes `--format text|json`; under `--json` stdout carries exactly one document — the framework envelope, whose `payload` member is the findings document. The document itself is unchanged, and the command declares its JSON Schema, so a deviating document fails the run instead of reaching a consumer. Every command now declares its effect, and the three that write files refuse `--dry-run` with the reason rather than previewing a rewrite they would not record.

### Features

- **`strictcode` CLI.** First command surface: `registry dump` writes the committed rule-registry artifact (REGISTRY.json); `matrix gen` writes the generated language-by-feature support matrix (docs/MATRIX.md).
- **The seed catalog, end-to-end.** `strictcode analyze` runs the eleven import-graph rules (dependency hygiene, dead code, cycles, config staleness, library boundary) over Python, Go, and TypeScript/JavaScript workspaces: text or JSON output, error findings fail the run, warnings do not. The 32-item lessons register is the acceptance suite.
- **Python full-semantic depth.** The graph now carries Python callables, classes (with protocol/enum classification), lambdas, containment, decorator and inheritance/ABC-register conformance edges, and syntactically resolved calls — dynamic dispatch stays honestly unresolved, never guessed. Completes the rule set: `library-stdout` (error), `library-direct-logging` (warning), and `unreachable-code` (error, all projects).
- **Tier-1 auto-fixes.** `strictcode fix --preview|--apply` removes unreachable statements — the transform is whitelisted, and every application is verified by re-extracting the graph and comparing it against the declared delta; a mismatch rolls the files back.
